name: VELCO Pinnacle Ridge, Rutland
heading: 3. VELCO Pinnacle Ridge, Rutland — Operating Grid Data Center; Capacity Undisclosed
brief: At 366 Pinnacle Ridge Road in Rutland , the Vermont Electric Power Company maintains a data center serving the state’s high-voltage transmission operations and communications. Unlike commercial colocation operators selling cabinets to outside customers, VELCO uses computing, monitoring and communications systems to help control grid equipment and manage the infrastructure that keeps utilities connected.

name: FirstLight Burlington/Williston
heading: 2. FirstLight Burlington/Williston — 20,000 Square Feet Listed; Operating
brief: FirstLight offers colocation and connectivity at 45 Krupp Drive in Williston , serving customers around greater Burlington. Data Center Map describes the facility as approximately 20,000 square feet , while the operator’s commercial listing describes redundant fiber routes, dual A/B power feeds, UPS and backup generation with five days of fuel storage.

name: Tech Vault, South Burlington
heading: 1. Tech Vault, South Burlington — 39,000 Square Feet Published; Operating
brief: The clearest space disclosure among the state’s identifiable commercial data centers comes from Tech Vault , which describes 39,000 square feet of data center space at 21 Gregory Drive in South Burlington . The operator says the carrier-neutral facility connects to six network providers and has independent cooling and electrical systems, multi-factor physical security, and support for colocation, managed services, backup and disaster recovery.

name: Digital Realty Digital Dulles, Sterling
heading: 5. Digital Realty Digital Dulles, Sterling — Up to 1 GW Planned; Operating and Expanding
brief: The Digital Realty development known as Digital Dulles occupies the former Western Lands property near Washington Dulles International Airport in Loudoun County. Digital Realty bought the approximately 424-acre parcel in 2018 and has been bringing large data halls into service since 2023. In a January 7, 2026 report , Data Center Dynamics said the operator had previously described a full-build campus of up to 1 GW supplied through six substations.

name: STACK Stafford Technology Campus
heading: 4. STACK Stafford Technology Campus — More Than 1 GW Planned; First Building Topped Out
brief: STACK Infrastructure is developing the Stafford Technology Campus along U.S. Route 1 and Eskimo Hill Road in Stafford County. At full development, the company says the roughly 500-acre campus is intended to contain 19 data center buildings with more than 1 GW of capacity . That is the developer’s long-term project target, not the load currently switched on.

name: EdgeCore Shannon Hill, Louisa County
heading: 3. EdgeCore Shannon Hill, Louisa County — More Than 1.1 GW Critical IT Planned
brief: EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure plans a large single-tenant campus at Shannon Hill Regional Business Park . The operator publishes more than 1.1 GW of eventual critical IT load , across approximately 697 acres and at least six data centers. Its current location sheet lists roughly 3.1 million square feet, although an earlier June 2025 announcement described approximately 3.9 million square feet. The difference reflects changing disclosed development scopes, not additional buildings that should b

name: Tract Hanover Technology Park
heading: 2. Tract Hanover Technology Park — 2.4 GW Master Plan; Site Infrastructure Underway
brief: Tract’s Hanover Technology Park covers approximately 1,211 acres near Ashland along Hickory Hill Road and Interstate 95. The developer says the property can support up to 2.4 GW of power capacity across a maximum of eight substations. Tract announced the acquisition in May 2024 after county supervisors approved the necessary industrial zoning and conditional use permissions earlier that year.

name: AWS Northeast Creek, Louisa County
heading: 1. AWS Northeast Creek, Louisa County — About 2.7 GW Tracked; Operating MW Unconfirmed
brief: The largest numerical figure in this selected comparison belongs to Amazon Web Services’ Northeast Creek Technology Campus , west of Jefferson Highway in Louisa County. A Virginia project directory assigns it approximately 2.7 GW of full-development site power , but the number should be treated as a third-party reported campus estimate , not an Amazon-certified critical IT rating or electricity currently consumed. The U.S. Army Corps’ 2024 filing does establish a project with ten data center bui

name: Microsoft Quincy Columbia
heading: 3. Microsoft Quincy Columbia — About 240 MW in a Third-Party Site Record; Operating
brief: Microsoft’s Quincy Columbia data center is a distinct facility in Grant County’s extensive cloud-computing hub. Data Center Record lists approximately 240 MW for its Quincy Columbia campus (MWH01), describing the facility as operating. That number is an attributed directory entry, not an independently recovered Microsoft technical specification . The record’s primary link identifies the Washington location but does not itself provide a readily retrievable 240 MW meter reading. Readers should tre

name: Microsoft Malaga, Chelan County
heading: 2. Microsoft Malaga, Chelan County — 288 MW Authorized Demand; Construction and Partial Service Reported
brief: In Malaga , just south of Wenatchee, Microsoft has been constructing a multi-building campus near the former Alcoa industrial property. The most authoritative number is in Chelan County Public Utility District’s June 2025 agreement summary : a maximum authorized demand of 288 MW under a 15-year large-load service arrangement covering August 2025 to July 2040. That is a contractual ceiling subject to supply and reliability conditions, not an assertion that 288 MW of hardware is running continuous

name: Microsoft Quincy MWH
heading: 1. Microsoft Quincy MWH — About 295 MW Modeled IT Capacity; Operating and Expanding
brief: Microsoft’s larger Quincy MWH campus ranks first among the three on the basis of an approximately 295 MW independent IT-power estimate published in a sample table by Cleanview . Its Washington market inventory also names Microsoft Quincy MWH as the state’s largest operating campus by its model of power associated with online buildings. This is researcher-modeled capacity, not a disclosed Microsoft utility meter or a guaranteed 2026 instantaneous IT draw. Differences in modeling methods and campu

name: Fundamental Data Ridgeline, Tucker County
heading: 3. Fundamental Data Ridgeline, Tucker County — About 1.6 GW Discussed; Roughly 785 MW Permitted Power
brief: The Ridgeline proposal would bring a privately powered data center development to a former mining area near Davis and Thomas, with possible expansion into Grant County. Developer Fundamental Data describes it as a combination of generation infrastructure and future computing capacity, but has not identified an operating data hall or publicly confirmed an AI tenant. The wider 1.6 GW figure appeared in reporting on an early project vision; it is not equivalent to a currently permitted, energized s

name: Starwood Project Tamarack, Mason County
heading: 2. Starwood Project Tamarack, Mason County — 2.16 GW Proposed; State Certified
brief: In West Columbia , about 20 miles north of Monarch, Starwood Digital Ventures is pursuing Project Tamarack , a separate large-scale campus. On September 3, 2026 , West Virginia’s governor announced high-impact data center certification for the project, stating that the development would require approximately 2.16 GW of electricity and involve $12 billion in planned investment . Certification is an important state decision, but it is neither proof of an operating facility nor a disclosure of crit

name: Nscale Monarch Compute Campus, Mason County
heading: 1. Nscale Monarch Compute Campus, Mason County — 8 GW Expansion Ambition; 2 GW First-Phase Power
brief: Nscale’s Monarch Compute Campus near Point Pleasant is West Virginia’s biggest disclosed AI infrastructure vision by long-term planned power scale. The company acquired the development in March 2026 and describes a site exceeding 2,250 acres , with an ultimate possible expansion to 8 GW or more . Phase One is much smaller: the state’s September 3 announcement refers to approximately 2 GW of power requirements , and the company identifies a 1.35 GW planned AI compute capacity target. Those number

name: Meta Beaver Dam
heading: 3. Meta Beaver Dam — 220 MW Projected Peak Demand; Under Construction
brief: Meta announced its first Wisconsin data center in Beaver Dam, Dodge County , on November 12, 2025. The planned AI-optimized campus will contain more than 700,000 square feet of facilities and represents at least $1 billion in investment . Alliant Energy’s initial project announcement anticipated roughly 1,000 construction jobs at peak and more than 100 long-term operational roles, with the data center expected to come online in 2027.

name: Microsoft Fairwater, Mount Pleasant
heading: 2. Microsoft Fairwater, Mount Pleasant — About 450 MW Tracked; First Facility Operating
brief: Microsoft announced on June 23 that its first Fairwater facility in Mount Pleasant was fully operational after equipment began coming online in April. The large AI computing campus occupies land once associated with Foxconn’s much smaller-than-promised Wisconsin manufacturing expansion. Microsoft said the first facility was supporting nearly 550 full-time jobs at the June milestone and that its second adjacent facility was under construction for anticipated completion in 2028.

name: Vantage Lighthouse, Port Washington
heading: 1. Vantage Lighthouse, Port Washington — 902 MW Critical IT Planned; Construction Underway
brief: The largest disclosed site-level critical IT plan in this selection is Vantage Data Centers’ Lighthouse campus near Lake Michigan in Port Washington. The company describes four data center buildings spanning 2.5 million square feet across 672 acres , with a planned 902 MW of critical IT load and targeted full completion in 2028. It is being developed to serve Oracle and OpenAI’s Stargate infrastructure. A different roughly 1.3 GW figure appears in electrical interconnection planning; that is not

name: Vantage Project Latigo, Laramie County
heading: 3. Vantage Project Latigo, Laramie County — 480 MW Proposed; Rezoning Approved
brief: Vantage Data Centers is seeking to develop Project Latigo on approximately 1,835 acres along Terry Ranch Road, about 12 miles south of Cheyenne. The project is described as a roughly 480 MW initial campus , with discussion of potential future expansion. A September 1, 2026 Laramie County commissioners meeting approved the land-use change to a Planned Unit Development on a unanimous vote. That authorizes a zoning framework; it does not mean data halls are built, a tenant has signed, or 480 MW is

name: Prometheus Hyperscale Evanston
heading: 2. Prometheus Hyperscale Evanston — 1.25 GW Initial Plan; County Permits Approved
brief: Prometheus Hyperscale is pursuing a 1.25 GW initial data center campus on approximately 506 acres east of Evanston in Uinta County. The developer has promoted a possible path to 5 GW through later expansion, but that larger number is not part of today’s initial ranking. On June 16 , county commissioners unanimously approved the conditional-use permit for the data center, according to the company’s June 17 announcement .

name: Google Project Tembo, Cheyenne
heading: 1. Google Project Tembo, Cheyenne — 2.7 GW Power-Resource Mix; Pre-Construction
brief: Google’s Project Tembo , located in the Switchgrass Industrial Park approximately eight miles south of Cheyenne, is tied to Wyoming’s largest disclosed data center power arrangement. The site was formerly Project Jade , a Crusoe-and-Tallgrass development initially described as a 1.8 GW computing project. Crusoe exited during 2026, and Google subsequently advanced a revised four-building concept. In September, the company presented the community with a planned investment of approximately $17 bill

name: Tract Caldwell Valley, Texas
heading: 10. Tract Caldwell Valley, Texas — 4 GW Site Capacity
brief: Tract’s Caldwell Valley Technology Park comprises nearly 3,000 acres in Caldwell County with roughly 4 GW of marketed development capacity . The campus combines planned data-center plots with prospective transmission and natural-gas infrastructure, but the master-plan number does not represent a signed four-gigawatt supply contract.

name: Joule High-Performance Compute Campus, Utah
heading: 9. Joule High-Performance Compute Campus, Utah — 4 GW Energy Plan
brief: Joule Capital Partners and Caterpillar have publicized a four-gigawatt total-energy design for a high-performance compute campus in Utah. Their approach centers on gas-powered distributed generation, integrated cooling and recovery of waste heat from equipment, rather than depending solely on distant grid deliveries.

name: Homer City Energy Campus, Pennsylvania
heading: 8. Homer City Energy Campus, Pennsylvania — Up to 4.4 GW Planned Power
brief: The redevelopment of Pennsylvania’s retired Homer City coal station is designed around up to 4.4 GW of natural-gas electricity generation for AI data centers and possible grid service. Some permitting and coverage use approximately 4.5 GW or a different equipment nameplate figure, illustrating how turbine ratings and project design assumptions can vary.

name: Meta Hyperion, Louisiana
heading: 7. Meta Hyperion, Louisiana — 5 GW Planned Compute Capacity
brief: Meta announced that its Richland Parish investment is being expanded toward 5 GW of compute capacity . Hyperion is already a major construction effort with associated transmission and electricity-supply work. The company’s target measures an eventual compute development scale, not proof of five gigawatts of operating servers in 2026.

name: E2B4 Roswell Information Park, New Mexico
heading: 6. E2B4 Roswell Information Park, New Mexico — 6.5 GW Proposed Generation
brief: E2B4’s proposed Roswell Information Park separates its engineering targets more clearly than many developers: its investor materials call for 6.5 GW of net islanded generation supporting 4,960 MW of critical IT capacity across 20 halls. That difference is important because the generators must also cover equipment losses, cooling requirements and reliability reserves.

name: Nscale Monarch Compute Campus, West Virginia
heading: 5. Nscale Monarch Compute Campus, West Virginia — Over 8 GW Power Runway
brief: Nscale’s proposed Monarch campus in Mason County has a long-term microgrid expansion runway exceeding 8 GW , according to its March announcement. The site has a state-certified development framework, but the large figure represents possible phased expansion rather than currently available electricity. Early project reporting described a much smaller roughly 2 GW first-phase ambition.

name: PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, Ohio
heading: 4. PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, Ohio — 8 GW Planned IT Load
brief: OpenAI says its partnership with SB Energy, NVIDIA and the U.S. Department of Energy targets approximately 8 GW of critical IT capacity near Piketon, at and around the former Portsmouth uranium-enrichment site. That figure measures electricity intended for computing equipment; the corresponding facility-level power requirement would be greater after cooling, power distribution and other overhead.

name: Stratos / Wonder Valley, Utah
heading: 3. Stratos / Wonder Valley, Utah — About 9 GW Long-Term Concept
brief: The Stratos Project Area in Box Elder County has been described by Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority at approximately 9 GW of long-run project scale. The developer’s more detailed Wonder Valley Utah disclosure discusses approximately 7.5 GW over later stages, while an October water application outlines fifteen 500 MW natural-gas blocks.

name: Creekstone Delta Gigasite, Utah
heading: 2. Creekstone Delta Gigasite, Utah — More Than 10 GW Power Stack
brief: Creekstone Energy says its proposed Delta Gigasite combines natural gas, solar and storage resources into a power stack exceeding 10 GW . The company’s breakdown includes 2.1 GW natural gas and 6 GW solar, along with storage and other resources. Storage capacity and intermittent solar nameplate output are not the same as continuous round-the-clock generation.

name: Fermi Project Matador, Texas
heading: 1. Fermi Project Matador, Texas — 11 GW Power Campus
brief: Fermi’s Project Matador near Amarillo is pursuing a vast, phased mix of natural gas, potential nuclear generation and grid-connected resources. The 11 GW headline describes an ultimate energy-campus design rather than installed power plants or operating data halls. Fermi’s latest annual report retains an 11 GW goal for the principal campus while describing possible expansion on additional acreage.
